b.title: Beyond the Milky Way
text: Edwin Hubble, born in Missouri on November 20, 1889, first studied law at Oxford before returning to his real passion: the stars.

In the early 1920s, astronomers were still arguing about whether fuzzy patches of light called nebulae were inside our galaxy or far beyond it. Using the giant Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson in California, Hubble measured special pulsing stars in the Andromeda nebula and showed that it was far too distant to belong to the Milky Way.
Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.

In 1929 Hubble published another landmark result: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away from us. This was strong evidence that the universe is expanding. The Belgian scientist Georges Lemaître had proposed a similar idea two years earlier, which is why the rule is now often called the Hubble–Lemaître law.
In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Hubble showed that other galaxies exist and that the universe is expanding.
Hubble studied law at Oxford before he turned to astronomy instead.
Lemaître built the giant Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson in California.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into orbit back in 1929.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：證明其他星系存在、宇宙在膨脹。

q.q: How did Hubble show Andromeda was outside the Milky Way?
opts: He took photos with the Hubble Space Telescope in 1990
He read Lemaître's paper and agreed with it
He measured pulsing stars and found it too far away
He took pictures of it with the space telescope
q.why: 第二段：measured special pulsing stars … far too distant。

q.q: What did Hubble publish in 1929?
opts: Andromeda is a cloud of gas inside our galaxy
The universe is slowly shrinking over time
The Milky Way is the only galaxy that exists
Farther galaxies seem to move away faster
q.why: 第四段：the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to be moving away。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “expanding” means ___.
opts: getting colder
getting bigger
staying the same
turning around
q.why: expanding = 擴張、變大。

q.q: Why is the rule now often called the Hubble–Lemaître law?
opts: Lemaître built the telescope Hubble used
The two scientists were brothers
NASA renamed the law in 1990
Lemaître proposed a similar idea earlier
q.why: 第四段：Lemaître had proposed a similar idea two years earlier。

q.q: A website says: “Hubble alone came up with the idea that the universe is expanding.” Based on the text, is this fair?
opts: Not fully — Lemaître proposed it two years earlier
Yes — nobody else had ever studied the question
Yes — the space telescope is named after him
No — Hubble studied law, not the stars
q.why: 第四段：勒梅特早兩年提出類似想法。

tr.en: Andromeda was a separate galaxy, and suddenly the universe was vastly larger than anyone had imagined.
tr.zh: 仙女座是一個獨立的星系，宇宙一下子變得比任何人想像的都大得多。

tr.en: This was strong evidence that the universe is expanding.
tr.zh: 這是宇宙正在膨脹的有力證據。

tr.en: In 1990 NASA launched a space telescope in his honour, which continues his work above Earth's blurry atmosphere.
tr.zh: 1990 年，NASA 發射了一架以他命名的太空望遠鏡，在地球模糊的大氣層之上延續他的工作。

tz: 愛德溫・哈伯 1889 年 11 月 20 日生於密蘇里州，他先在牛津大學讀法律，後來才回到他真正熱愛的事物：星星。
在 1920 年代初期，天文學家仍在爭論那些叫做「星雲」的模糊光斑，究竟是在我們的銀河系裡面，還是遠在它之外。哈伯使用加州威爾遜山上巨大的胡克望遠鏡，測量仙女座星雲中一種特殊的脈動星，證明它距離太遠，不可能屬於銀河系。
仙女座是一個獨立的星系——宇宙一下子變得比任何人想像的都大得多。
1929 年，哈伯發表了另一項里程碑般的成果：一個星系離我們越遠，它遠離我們的速度看起來就越快。這是宇宙正在膨脹的有力證據。比利時科學家喬治・勒梅特在兩年前就提出過類似的想法，所以這條規律現在常被稱為「哈伯－勒梅特定律」。
1990 年，美國太空總署發射了一架以他命名的太空望遠鏡，在地球模糊的大氣層之上延續他的研究。

ph.ex: The box is far too heavy for me.
ph.exzh: 這個箱子對我來說實在太重了。

ph.ex: Which team do you belong to?
ph.exzh: 你屬於哪一隊？

ph.ex: The more you read, the better you write.
ph.exzh: 讀得越多，寫得越好。
ph.m: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster

ph.ex: A statue was built in her honour.
ph.exzh: 人們為紀念她建了一座雕像。

ph.ex: The plane flew above the clouds.
ph.exzh: 飛機在雲層之上飛行。

c.title: How Big Is Everything?
text: A century ago, the most basic question in astronomy, how big the universe is, had no agreed answer. Many astronomers believed the Milky Way contained everything; the faint spiral 'nebulae' scattered across the sky were assumed to be clouds within it.

Edwin Hubble, born on November 20, 1889, settled the dispute. In 1923, working with the great Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson, he identified a Cepheid variable, a star whose regular pulsing reveals its true brightness, in the Andromeda nebula. Comparing true and apparent brightness yielded a distance far beyond our galaxy's edge.
The implication was staggering: Andromeda was an 'island universe', and the cosmos contained countless such galaxies.

Six years later he went further, showing that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance. The universe was not static but expanding, a conclusion the Belgian priest-physicist Georges Lemaître had already reached theoretically, which is why astronomers now speak of the Hubble–Lemaître law.

Hubble never won a Nobel Prize, which did not then recognise astronomy. Yet his findings demoted humanity twice, from the centre of a single galaxy to one corner of an expanding cosmos, and few scientific discoveries have so thoroughly rescaled our sense of home.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Hubble's main achievement was finally winning the Nobel Prize in Physics.
Hubble proved the Milky Way is the whole universe, which made humans feel more central.
Hubble revealed countless galaxies in an expanding universe, shrinking our place.
The Milky Way, as people once thought, contains everything in the universe.
q.why: 主旨：無數星系＋宇宙膨脹，徹底改變人類的定位。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “recede” means ___.
opts: grow brighter
move away
stop moving
explode
q.why: recede = 後退、遠離。

q.q: Why was the Cepheid variable star so useful?
opts: It was simply the brightest star in the whole night sky
It was located safely inside our own Milky Way galaxy
It proved once and for all that the universe is static
Its regular pulsing shows its true brightness, so distance
q.why: 第二段：its regular pulsing reveals its true brightness——比較真實與視亮度可推算距離。

q.q: How does the writer view Hubble's lack of a Nobel Prize?
opts: A technicality that doesn't reduce his work
Proof that his work was really quite minor
Deeply unfair to the scientist Lemaître
A mistake made by NASA in naming the telescope
q.why: 第五段：諾貝爾獎當時不包含天文學，但他的發現依然極重要（Yet …）。

q.q: What does the phrase “demoted humanity twice” refer to?
opts: Two important prizes that Hubble failed to win
Two different telescopes that Hubble used
Two public arguments he had with Lemaître
Two discoveries that each made our place smaller
q.why: 結尾：從單一星系的中心，降為膨脹宇宙中的一角。

q.q: Which piece of evidence was MOST important for proving Andromeda is outside the Milky Way?
opts: A beautiful photo showing Andromeda's spiral shape
Distance worked out from a Cepheid's true brightness
Hubble's law degree from the University of Oxford
The size of the mirror in the Hooker telescope
q.why: 第二段：用造父變星的真實與視亮度算出距離，才證明它在銀河系之外。

tz: 一個世紀以前，天文學最基本的問題——宇宙有多大——還沒有公認的答案。許多天文學家相信銀河系就包含了一切；散布在天空中那些微弱的螺旋狀「星雲」，被認為是銀河系裡的雲氣。
1889 年 11 月 20 日出生的愛德溫・哈伯，解決了這場爭論。1923 年，他使用威爾遜山上偉大的胡克望遠鏡，在仙女座星雲中找到一顆造父變星——一種規律脈動、能透露出自身真實亮度的恆星。比較它的真實亮度和看起來的亮度，就算出一個遠遠超出銀河系邊界的距離。
這個結論驚人至極：仙女座是一個「島宇宙」，而宇宙中有無數個這樣的星系。
六年後他更進一步，證明星系遠離的速度和它們的距離成正比。宇宙不是靜止的，而是在膨脹——比利時的神父兼物理學家喬治・勒梅特早已在理論上得出這個結論，這就是為什麼天文學家現在稱它為「哈伯－勒梅特定律」。
哈伯從未獲得諾貝爾獎，因為當時諾貝爾獎不頒給天文學。然而，他的發現兩度把人類「降級」：從一個星系的中心，降到一個不斷膨脹的宇宙裡的一個角落；很少有科學發現能如此徹底地改變我們對「家」的尺度感。

topic: World Fisheries Day
zh: 世界漁業日：海裡的魚還夠吃嗎？
src: FAO · Nature · Taipei Times

a.title: Fish for Tomorrow
text: November 21 is World Fisheries Day. It reminds us to take care of the fish in our seas, rivers and lakes.
Fish are an important food for billions of people. Millions of people also work as fishers.
But some people catch too many fish. Then there are not enough young fish to grow up and lay eggs. This is called overfishing.
Today, more than one third of the world's fish groups are overfished.
Some fish now come from fish farms. Farms can help, but they must be clean and careful too.
If we only catch what the sea can replace, there will be fish for our children in the future.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why people should stop eating any fish from the sea
Why fish farms are always bad for the sea
Caring for fish so there are enough in future
A big fishing competition held every year
q.why: 全文談保護魚類，讓未來還有魚可吃。

q.q: What is overfishing?
opts: Eating fish for dinner every single day
Catching so many fish that too few grow up
Building lots of fish farms along the coast
Fishing only in rivers and not in the sea
q.why: 第三段：catch too many fish … This is called overfishing。

q.q: How much of the world's fish groups are overfished?
opts: More than one third
Less than one tenth
All of them
Exactly a half
q.why: 第四段：more than one third。

q.q: In the text, “replace” means ___.
opts: throw something away in the bin
sell something at the market
catch something faster than before
put back or grow again what was taken
q.why: replace = 補回。

q.q: What does the writer think about fish farms?
opts: They can help, but must be clean and careful
They solve every problem the oceans have
They are perfect and solve every problem at sea
They are really the same as overfishing
q.why: 第五段：Farms can help, but they must be clean and careful too。

q.q: Your family is buying fish at the market. Based on the text, which choice helps the sea most?
opts: As many baby fish as you can find at the market
As much fish as possible while the price is low
Only fish that has come from very far away
Fish caught in a way that lets young fish grow
q.why: 第三、六段：讓小魚長大，只捕大海能補回的量。

gt.en: Fish are an important food for billions of people.
gt.zh: 魚是數十億人重要的食物。

gt.en: This is called overfishing.
gt.zh: 這叫做過度捕撈。

gt.en: Farms can help, but they must be clean and careful too.
gt.zh: 養殖場可以幫忙，但也必須乾淨又小心。

gt.zh: 如果我們只捕撈大海能補回的量，未來我們的孩子就還有魚。

tz: 11 月 21 日是世界漁業日。它提醒我們要照顧海洋、河川和湖泊裡的魚。
魚是好幾十億人重要的食物，也有數百萬人以捕魚為業。
但是有些人捕了太多魚。這樣一來，就沒有足夠的小魚能長大、產卵。這就叫做過度捕撈。
今天，全世界超過三分之一的魚群遭到過度捕撈。
現在有些魚來自養殖場。養殖場能幫上忙，但也必須乾淨、謹慎地經營。
如果我們只捕撈大海能補充回來的數量，將來我們的孩子也會有魚可以吃。

ph.ex: We must take care of the oceans.
ph.exzh: 我們必須好好照顧海洋。

ph.ex: My uncle works as a nurse.
ph.exzh: 我叔叔是一名護理師。

ph.ex: Baby turtles grow up fast.
ph.exzh: 小海龜長得很快。

ph.ex: In the future, I want to travel the world.
ph.exzh: 將來我想環遊世界。

b.title: Can the Oceans Keep Feeding Us?
text: World Fisheries Day, celebrated on November 21, was started in 1997 by fishing communities who met in New Delhi to call for responsible fishing around the world.
Fish and seafood are a major source of protein for billions of people, and fishing supports the jobs of tens of millions more, from small boats to large factory ships.

However, the oceans are under pressure. According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, more than a third of the world's fish stocks are now overfished, meaning they are caught faster than they can reproduce.
Illegal fishing, harmful methods that destroy the seabed, and bycatch, the accidental capture of dolphins, turtles and sharks, make the problem worse.
Fish farming, or aquaculture, now produces more than half of the seafood we eat. It can reduce pressure on wild fish, but poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters.
Experts say the solution includes catch limits, protected marine areas and better tracking of where fish come from.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Fish feed billions, and new fish farms have now completely ended overfishing.
Fish feed billions, but overfishing threatens the seas, so care is needed.
Fish farming has now completely solved the problem of overfishing.
Dolphins and sea turtles are caught as food for millions of people.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：魚很重要、海洋受威脅、需要負責任的漁業。

q.q: What does “overfished” mean in the text?
opts: Fish are caught faster than they can breed
There are too many fish farms in one area
The fish being caught are much too big
Fish are caught only by small local boats
q.why: 第三段：caught faster than they can reproduce。

q.q: How much of our seafood now comes from aquaculture?
opts: About a tenth
None
More than half
Exactly a third
q.why: 第五段：now produces more than half of the seafood we eat。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “bycatch” means ___.
opts: fish that are sold at local markets
fish that are raised on fish farms
fish that are caught on purpose to sell at markets
animals caught by accident while fishing
q.why: bycatch = 混獲，意外捕到的動物。

q.q: Why does the writer say fish farms are not a perfect solution?
opts: They produce far too little fish to feed people
They often catch dolphins and turtles by accident
Poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters
They are against the law in most countries
q.why: 第五段：poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters。

q.q: A seafood ad says: “Eat all the farmed fish you want — it never harms the ocean.” Based on the text, is this accurate?
opts: No — poorly run farms can pollute coastal waters
Yes — fish farms never cause any harm to the ocean
Yes — fish farms produce half of our seafood
No — farmed fish are not really fish at all
q.why: 第五段：管理不善的養殖場會汙染沿岸海水。

tr.en: However, the oceans are under pressure.
tr.zh: 然而，海洋正承受壓力。

tr.en: It can reduce pressure on wild fish, but poorly managed farms can pollute coastal waters.
tr.zh: 它能減輕野生魚類的壓力，但管理不善的養殖場會汙染沿岸海水。

tr.en: Experts say the solution includes catch limits, protected marine areas and better tracking of where fish come from.
tr.zh: 專家說，解決方法包括捕撈限額、海洋保護區，以及更完善地追蹤魚的來源。

tz: 每年 11 月 21 日的世界漁業日，始於 1997 年；當時各地的漁業社群在新德里聚會，呼籲全世界負責任地捕魚。
魚和海鮮是數十億人重要的蛋白質來源，而漁業從小船到大型加工船，支撐著數千萬人的工作。
然而，海洋正承受壓力。根據聯合國糧食及農業組織的資料，全世界超過三分之一的魚群如今遭到過度捕撈，也就是被捕撈的速度比牠們繁殖的速度還快。
非法捕魚、破壞海床的有害漁法，以及「混獲」——意外捕到海豚、海龜和鯊魚——都讓問題更加嚴重。
魚類養殖如今生產了我們所吃海鮮的一半以上。它可以減輕野生魚群的壓力，但管理不善的養殖場可能污染沿海水域。
專家說，解決方法包括限制捕撈量、設立海洋保護區，以及更完善地追蹤魚的來源。

ph.ex: Students called for longer lunch breaks.
ph.exzh: 學生們要求延長午休時間。

ph.ex: Many forests are under pressure from farming.
ph.exzh: 許多森林受到農業的壓力。

ph.ex: Shouting will only make things worse.
ph.exzh: 大吼只會讓事情更糟。

ph.ex: More than half of the class likes science.
ph.exzh: 班上超過一半的人喜歡自然科學。

ph.ex: Planting trees reduces pressure on wild forests.
ph.exzh: 種樹能減輕對野生森林的壓力。

c.title: The Tragedy of the Open Sea
text: The ocean once seemed inexhaustible. Today, World Fisheries Day, marked each November 21 since 1997, serves as an annual reminder that it is not.

According to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization, more than a third of assessed fish stocks are overfished, harvested faster than they can replenish themselves. The causes are partly technological: sonar, vast nets and subsidised fleets allow fishers to locate and remove fish with an efficiency earlier generations could not imagine.

Economists describe the dynamic as a 'tragedy of the commons'. Because no single fisher owns the sea, each has an incentive to catch as much as possible before others do, even though restraint would leave everyone better off.

Aquaculture has eased some pressure and now supplies most of the seafood humans eat, but it brings its own costs, including coastal pollution and, for some species, a reliance on wild fish ground into feed.

The most promising answers are institutional rather than technical: enforceable quotas, marine reserves where stocks can recover, and traceability that lets consumers reward responsible fleets. The sea can recover remarkably quickly, but only if people agree to share it.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Better fishing technology will, on its own, solve the overfishing problem.
Fish farming offers a way to feed people with no costs at all.
Overfishing is a shared-resource problem needing rules and cooperation.
The ocean is so vast that its fish can never really run out.
q.why: 主旨：這是公共資源問題，要靠可執行的制度與合作。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “incentive” means ___.
opts: a type of large fishing net
a law that limits fishing
a law that punishes people for fishing
a reason that encourages an action
q.why: incentive = 誘因。

q.q: Why does each fisher catch as much as possible, according to the 'tragedy of the commons'?
opts: Fishing has become very easy with modern boats
No one owns the sea, so each fears others will take it
Fish are cheap, so fishers must catch a lot
Quotas require each fisher to catch as much as possible
q.why: 第三段：no single fisher owns the sea … catch as much as possible before others do。

q.q: How does the writer view aquaculture?
opts: As helpful, but with its own costs
As a perfect solution for the seas
As completely harmful to the ocean
As illegal in most countries
q.why: 第四段：has eased some pressure … but it brings its own costs。

q.q: What does the final sentence suggest?
opts: Recovery is possible, but needs cooperation
The sea can no longer recover from fishing
Technology alone will save the world's fish
Consumers should simply stop eating fish
q.why: 結尾：can recover … but only if people agree to share it。

q.q: Three countries share one sea. Which plan best follows the writer's advice?
opts: Each country builds faster boats to catch more first
All three countries stop eating fish completely
Agree limits, set up a reserve, and track sales
They let each fisher decide how much to catch
q.why: 最後一段：enforceable quotas, marine reserves … traceability。

tz: 海洋曾經看似取之不盡。如今，自 1997 年起每年 11 月 21 日舉行的世界漁業日，每年都提醒我們：事實並非如此。
根據聯合國糧食及農業組織的資料，在接受評估的魚群中，超過三分之一遭到過度捕撈，被捕撈的速度快過牠們自我補充的速度。原因有一部分在於科技：聲納、巨大的漁網和政府補貼的船隊，讓漁民能以前人無法想像的效率找到並撈走魚群。
經濟學家把這種情況稱為「公地悲劇」。因為沒有任何一個漁民擁有大海，每個人都有誘因在別人之前盡量多捕一些，儘管大家都節制反而會讓所有人過得更好。
水產養殖減輕了一些壓力，如今供應了人類所吃的大部分海鮮，但它也有自己的代價，包括沿海污染；某些魚種還依賴用野生魚磨成的飼料。
最有希望的解答在於制度，而不是技術：可以落實執行的捕撈配額、讓魚群得以恢復的海洋保護區，以及讓消費者能夠支持負責任船隊的產銷履歷。大海恢復的速度可以快得驚人，但前提是人們願意一起分享它。

ph.ex: The old school now serves as a museum.
ph.exzh: 這所舊學校現在作為博物館使用。

ph.ex: We use water faster than rain can refill it.
ph.exzh: 我們用水的速度比雨水補充得還快。

ph.ex: Sign up early, before others do.
ph.exzh: 趁別人還沒報名前，早點報名。

ph.ex: Sharing the work leaves everyone better off.
ph.exzh: 分工合作讓每個人都輕鬆一點。

ph.ex: A day off can ease pressure on tired students.
ph.exzh: 放一天假能減輕疲累學生的壓力。

ph.ex: Choose fruit rather than sweets.
ph.exzh: 選水果，而不是甜食。

ph.ex: You can borrow my bike, but only if you bring it back by six.
ph.exzh: 你可以借我的腳踏車，但只有在六點前還回來的情況下。

Why is it hard to stop overfishing when the sea belongs to no one?

topic: King Midas and the Golden Touch
zh: 點石成金的邁達斯王
src: Ovid's Metamorphoses · Smithsonian · BBC

a.title: Be Careful What You Wish For
text: Long ago, in a Greek story, there was a king named Midas. He loved gold more than anything.
One day, Midas helped a friend of the god Dionysus. To thank him, the god gave Midas one wish.
Midas said, 'I wish that everything I touch turns into gold!' His wish came true.
At first he was very happy. He touched a stone, a flower and a chair, and they all became gold.
But then he tried to eat. His bread and water turned into gold too! Midas was hungry and afraid.
He asked the god to take the gift back. Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?
opts: How the king's cooks made bread and wine
A king whose golden wish caused trouble
A friend of the god Dionysus who got lost
Why gold is such a beautiful metal
q.why: 全文講邁達斯的點金願望帶來麻煩。

q.q: Why did the god give Midas a wish?
opts: Midas loved gold more than anything
Midas was very hungry and thirsty
Midas helped the god's friend
Midas was a god himself
q.why: 第二段：Midas helped a friend of the god Dionysus. To thank him …

q.q: What happened when Midas tried to eat?
opts: His bread and water turned into gold
His food began to taste much better
He became a god who could fly
He found even more gold in the river
q.why: 第五段：His bread and water turned into gold too!

q.q: In the text, “touch” means ___.
opts: look at something closely
eat something quickly
buy something at a shop
put your hand on something
q.why: touch = 碰觸。

q.q: What lesson did Midas learn?
opts: Gold is the most important thing of all
The gods never help ordinary people
Some things are worth more than gold
Wishes always make people happy
q.why: 最後一段：some things are worth more than gold。

q.q: A classmate says, “If I were rich, I would never have any problems.” What would Midas's story suggest?
opts: Money can't buy everything, like food and love
You are right — gold solves every problem
You should ask a god to give you money
You are right — being rich solves every problem
q.why: 故事寓意：金錢買不到所有真正重要的東西。

gt.en: He loved gold more than anything.
gt.zh: 他愛黃金勝過一切。

gt.en: To thank him, the god gave Midas one wish.
gt.zh: 為了感謝他，神給了邁達斯一個願望。

gt.en: His wish came true.
gt.zh: 他的願望實現了。

gt.en: Midas learned that some things are worth more than gold.
gt.zh: 邁達斯學到，有些東西比黃金更有價值。

tz: 很久以前，在一個希臘故事裡，有一位名叫邁達斯的國王。他愛黃金勝過一切。
有一天，邁達斯幫助了酒神戴歐尼修斯的一位朋友。為了感謝他，酒神給了邁達斯一個願望。
邁達斯說：「我希望我碰到的每樣東西都變成黃金！」他的願望實現了。
一開始他非常開心。他摸了一顆石頭、一朵花和一張椅子，它們全都變成了黃金。
但接著他想吃東西。他的麵包和水也變成了黃金！邁達斯又餓又害怕。
他請求酒神把這份禮物收回去。邁達斯學到了：有些東西比黃金更有價值。

ph.ex: She loves her dog more than anything.
ph.exzh: 她愛她的狗勝過一切。

ph.ex: I hope your dream comes true.
ph.exzh: 希望你的夢想成真。

ph.ex: The caterpillar turned into a butterfly.
ph.exzh: 毛毛蟲變成了蝴蝶。

ph.ex: I'm sorry — I take back what I said.
ph.exzh: 對不起，我收回我說的話。

b.title: The Curse of the Golden Touch
text: In Greek mythology, Midas was a wealthy king of Phrygia who believed that more gold would bring him more happiness.

When Midas kindly looked after Silenus, the old teacher of the wine god Dionysus, the grateful god offered him any reward he desired. Without hesitating, Midas asked that everything he touched would turn to gold.

At first the gift seemed wonderful. Twigs, stones and apples glittered in his hands. But when he sat down to dinner, his bread hardened into metal and his wine became liquid gold. The richest man in the world was starving.
Desperate, Midas begged Dionysus to undo the wish. The god told him to wash in the River Pactolus, and according to the myth, that is why the river's sand sparkled with gold ever after.
In a famous later retelling by the American writer Nathaniel Hawthorne, Midas even turns his beloved daughter into a golden statue — a detail that makes the warning hit harder.
Today, the phrase 'the Midas touch' describes someone whose projects always make money, though the original story is really a warning about greed.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The American writer Hawthorne wrote the very first story about Midas.
The River Pactolus is still full of gold that people can find today.
Midas's golden wish showed how greed destroys what truly matters.
Dionysus was the Greek god in charge of gold and wealth.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：貪婪的願望毀掉真正重要的東西。

q.q: Why did Dionysus offer Midas a reward?
opts: Midas gave the god a large gift of gold
Midas won a race against the other kings
Midas was really the god's own son
Midas looked after Silenus, his old teacher
q.why: 第二段：Midas kindly looked after Silenus。

q.q: How did Midas get rid of the golden touch?
opts: He gave all of his gold away
He washed in the River Pactolus
He broke the golden statue
He stopped eating and drinking
q.why: 第四段：wash in the River Pactolus。

q.q: In paragraph 6, “greed” means ___.
opts: wanting much more than you need
great kindness to others
deep and lasting sadness
wanting to share what you have with others
q.why: greed = 貪婪。

q.q: Why does the writer say Hawthorne's daughter detail “makes the warning hit harder”?
opts: Golden statues are very expensive to make
Losing someone he loved shows greed's true cost
Hawthorne was an American, not a Greek
Golden statues show how beautiful the king's wish was
q.why: 第五段：把心愛的女兒變成金像，貪婪的代價更沉重。

q.q: A news article praises a businessman for having “the Midas touch.” Based on the text, what is surprising about this phrase?
opts: Today it's praise, but the story warns against greed
It means the businessman is very kind to others
Today it's a warning, but the story praises greed
It means the businessman is a kind of god
q.why: 最後一段：今天是讚美賺錢能力，原故事其實是對貪婪的警告。

tr.en: At first the gift seemed wonderful.
tr.zh: 一開始，這份禮物看起來好極了。

tr.en: The richest man in the world was starving.
tr.zh: 世界上最有錢的人卻在挨餓。

tr.en: Desperate, Midas begged Dionysus to undo the wish.
tr.zh: 走投無路的邁達斯懇求戴奧尼索斯收回這個願望。

tz: 在希臘神話中，邁達斯是弗里吉亞一位富有的國王，他相信更多的黃金會帶給他更多的快樂。
邁達斯好心照顧了酒神戴歐尼修斯的老師西勒諾斯，心懷感激的酒神願意給他任何他想要的報答。邁達斯毫不猶豫地要求：凡是他碰到的東西都要變成黃金。
一開始，這份禮物似乎好極了。樹枝、石頭和蘋果在他手中閃閃發亮。但當他坐下來吃晚餐時，麵包硬成了金屬，酒也變成了液態的黃金。世界上最富有的人，卻快要餓死了。
走投無路的邁達斯懇求戴歐尼修斯取消這個願望。酒神叫他到帕克托羅斯河裡洗澡；根據神話，這就是那條河的沙子從此閃著金光的原因。
在美國作家納撒尼爾・霍桑一個著名的改寫版本中，邁達斯甚至把他心愛的女兒變成了一座金像——這個細節讓故事的警告更加震撼。
今天，「點金術（the Midas touch）」這個說法用來形容做什麼都能賺錢的人，雖然原本的故事其實是一個關於貪婪的警告。

ph.ex: Can you look after my plants while I'm away?
ph.exzh: 我不在時，你可以幫我照顧植物嗎？

ph.ex: We sat down to dinner at seven.
ph.exzh: 我們七點坐下來吃晚餐。

ph.ex: He begged his mum to let him stay up late.
ph.exzh: 他懇求媽媽讓他晚點睡。

ph.ex: They lived happily ever after.
ph.exzh: 他們從此過著幸福快樂的日子。

ph.zh: 點石成金的本事（做什麼都賺錢）
ph.ex: She has the Midas touch — every shop she opens is a success.
ph.exzh: 她有點石成金的本事，開的每家店都很成功。

c.title: The Poverty of Gold
text: Few myths compress a moral so neatly as that of King Midas. Granted a wish by Dionysus in gratitude for sheltering the god's elderly companion Silenus, the Phrygian king asks that whatever he touches be turned to gold, and discovers at dinner that he has made himself unable to eat.

The story's force lies in its precise inversion. Gold is valuable precisely because it can be exchanged for other things; Midas, by converting everything into gold, abolishes the very things gold was meant to buy. His wealth becomes a form of poverty.

Ancient versions, preserved most famously by the Roman poet Ovid, end with Midas washing away his curse in the River Pactolus, an aetiological flourish explaining the gold-bearing sands of a real river.
Later tellers sharpened the tale. Nathaniel Hawthorne's nineteenth-century version adds a daughter who turns to metal at her father's embrace, shifting the moral from hunger to love.

Curiously, modern English has reversed the myth's meaning. To have 'the Midas touch' is now a compliment for commercial success, as though the cautionary half of the story had been quietly edited out — perhaps the most telling evidence of how persuasive the dream of endless wealth remains.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Midas was, above all, a successful king who knew how to make money.
Ovid invented the River Pactolus to explain where Midas's gold went.
The myth praises wealth, and our language has kept that meaning of praise.
The myth shows wealth becoming poverty, yet our language made it praise.
q.why: 主旨：財富變貧窮的寓言，現代英文卻把警告變成讚美。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “cautionary” means ___.
opts: very funny
about money
giving a warning
from ancient Rome
q.why: cautionary = 警示性的。

q.q: What does the writer mean by “His wealth becomes a form of poverty”?
opts: Turning all to gold destroys what gold should buy
Midas soon loses all of the gold that he has
Midas gives all of his gold to the poor people of his land
Midas gives all of his gold to the poor
q.why: 第二段：把一切變成黃金，反而消滅了黃金能買的東西。

q.q: How does the writer view the modern phrase 'the Midas touch'?
opts: As a correct summary of the myth's lesson
As an ironic reversal showing wealth's pull
As an insult to successful business people
As a phrase first used by Ovid himself
q.why: 最後一段：反轉神話原意——顯示無盡財富的夢多麼誘人。

q.q: What is the role of paragraph 4 (Hawthorne's version)?
opts: To prove that Ovid's version was wrong
To explain where the River Pactolus is
To show how retellings moved the moral to love
To show that Hawthorne kept Ovid's moral exactly the same
q.why: 第四段：shifting the moral from hunger to love。

q.q: An app promises: “Turn all your free time into money!” Based on the essay, what would be the strongest criticism?
opts: Turning everything into money can destroy rest and relationships
The app might not actually make you enough money in the end
Apps on phones are not really able to make money for anyone
The app might not actually turn enough of your free time into money
q.why: 第二段的邏輯：把一切換成金錢，反而失去金錢本來要換取的東西。

tz: 很少有神話能像邁達斯國王的故事一樣，把一個寓意濃縮得如此精準。弗里吉亞國王因為收留了酒神戴歐尼修斯年邁的同伴西勒諾斯，獲得酒神賜予一個願望；他要求凡是他碰到的東西都變成黃金，卻在晚餐時發現，自己讓自己再也吃不了東西。
這個故事的力量在於它精準的反轉。黃金之所以有價值，正是因為它能換到其他東西；而邁達斯把一切都變成黃金，等於消滅了黃金本來要用來購買的那些東西。他的財富變成了一種貧窮。
古代的版本——最有名的是由羅馬詩人奧維德保存下來的——結局是邁達斯在帕克托羅斯河裡洗去詛咒，用一段解釋來源的情節，說明了一條真實河流裡為什麼有含金的沙子。
後來的說書人讓故事更加尖銳。納撒尼爾・霍桑在十九世紀的版本加入了一個女兒，她在父親擁抱時變成了金屬，把寓意從飢餓轉向了愛。
奇妙的是，現代英文把這則神話的意思反了過來。擁有「點金術」如今是稱讚一個人生意成功，彷彿故事裡警告的那一半被悄悄刪掉了——這或許是最能說明「無盡財富」的夢想至今仍多麼誘人的證據。

ph.ex: She sent flowers in gratitude for their help.
ph.exzh: 她送花感謝他們的幫忙。

ph.ex: Points can be exchanged for small gifts.
ph.exzh: 點數可以兌換小禮物。

ph.ex: Dancing is a form of exercise.
ph.exzh: 跳舞是一種運動。

ph.ex: The teacher shifted our focus from grammar to speaking.
ph.exzh: 老師把我們的重點從文法轉到口說。
ph.m: shifting the moral from hunger to love

ph.ex: The funny part was edited out of the video.
ph.exzh: 好笑的那段被剪掉了。

ph.ex: He talks as though he knows everything.
ph.exzh: 他說話的樣子好像什麼都懂。

discuss: If you could have one magic power for a day, what would you choose — and could it go wrong?
What are some things that are 'worth more than gold' to you?
Why do you think people today use 'the Midas touch' as praise?

topic: World Children's Day: Rights for Every Child
zh: 世界兒童日：每個孩子的權利
src: UNICEF · United Nations · Taipei Times

a.title: Every Child Has Rights
text: November 20 is World Children's Day. On this day in 1989, the United Nations agreed on a special promise for children.
It is called the Convention on the Rights of the Child. A right is something every person should have.
Children have the right to go to school, to be safe, to see a doctor, and to play.
Children also have the right to give their opinions. Adults should listen when decisions are about them.
Almost every country in the world has signed this promise. Taiwan also made it part of its own laws in 2014.
But many children still cannot go to school or are not safe. World Children's Day reminds us to keep this promise.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How children should play games at school
World Children's Day and every child's rights
World Children's Day and the rights only adults have
How to see a doctor when you are ill
q.why: 全文介紹世界兒童日與兒童權利。

q.q: What happened on November 20, 1989?
opts: Taiwan made a new law about children
Every child in the world went to school
World Children's Day came to an end
The UN agreed on a promise for children
q.why: 第一段：the United Nations agreed on a special promise for children。

q.q: Which is NOT listed as a right in the text?
opts: To have their own car
To go to school
To play
To give their opinions
q.why: 第三、四段列出上學、安全、看醫生、玩、表達意見，沒有車子。

q.q: In the text, a “right” is ___.
opts: the opposite of the word left
a kind of game that children play
something every person should have
a rule that every school must follow
q.why: 第二段：A right is something every person should have。

q.q: Why does the day still matter today?
opts: Every child in the world can now go to school and is always safe
Many children still can't go to school or are not safe
The promise made in 1989 has now come to an end
Only adults, and not children, have any rights
q.why: 最後一段：many children still cannot go to school or are not safe。

q.q: Your school is choosing a new lunch menu. Based on the text, what should the school do?
opts: Decide quickly without asking any of the students
Let only the parents choose what children eat
Ask students, because the decision is about them
Choose the cheapest food without asking anyone
q.why: 第四段：Adults should listen when decisions are about them。

gt.en: A right is something every person should have.
gt.zh: 權利是每個人都應該擁有的東西。

gt.en: Children have the right to go to school, to be safe, to see a doctor, and to play.
gt.zh: 兒童有權上學、有權安全、有權看醫生，也有權玩耍。

gt.en: Adults should listen when decisions are about them.
gt.zh: 當決定和兒童有關時，大人應該聆聽。

gt.en: Taiwan also made it part of its own laws in 2014.
gt.zh: 台灣也在 2014 年把它納入自己的法律。

tz: 11 月 20 日是世界兒童日。1989 年的這一天，聯合國通過了一項給孩子的特別承諾。
它叫做《兒童權利公約》。「權利」是每個人都應該擁有的東西。
孩子有權利上學、有權利安全、有權利看醫生，也有權利玩耍。
孩子也有權利表達自己的意見。當決定和孩子有關時，大人應該仔細聽。
世界上幾乎每個國家都簽署了這項承諾。台灣也在 2014 年把它納入自己的法律。
但是仍有許多孩子無法上學，或生活得不安全。世界兒童日提醒我們要遵守這個承諾。

ph.ex: We finally agreed on a name for our team.
ph.exzh: 我們終於決定了隊名。

ph.ex: Everyone can give their opinion in class.
ph.exzh: 每個人在課堂上都可以發表意見。

ph.ex: This book is about friendship.
ph.exzh: 這本書是關於友誼的。

ph.ex: Always keep your promises.
ph.exzh: 一定要遵守你的承諾。

b.title: A Promise to the World's Children
text: On November 20, 1989, the United Nations adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child, and the date is now celebrated as World Children's Day.

The convention sets out the rights that every person under 18 should enjoy, wherever they live. They include the right to education, to health care, to protection from violence and exploitation, and, in a famous article, the right to rest and play.

One of its most important ideas is that children are not just people to be protected. They have the right to express their views on matters that affect them, and adults must take those views seriously.

It has become the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history: every UN member state except the United States has ratified it. Taiwan, which is not a UN member, passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its own legal system.
Yet the gap between promise and reality remains wide. Millions of children are still out of school, working in dangerous jobs, or living through war.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The United States is the only UN member that has not ratified the convention.
The 1989 convention promises every child rights, but many still lack them.
Taiwan passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its legal system.
Children need protection from harm more than they need a voice in decisions.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：公約承諾權利與發聲，但現實仍有落差。

q.q: Who is a “child” under the convention?
opts: Anyone under 12
Only students
Every person under 18
Anyone who lives with parents
q.why: 第二段：every person under 18。

q.q: How did Taiwan respond to the convention?
opts: It passed a 2014 law making it part of its legal system
It ratified the convention at the UN in 1989
It joined the UN in 2014 and signed the convention there at once
It wrote the first draft of the convention
q.why: 第四段：passed a law in 2014。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “ratified” means ___.
opts: completely rejected
written by children
translated into English
officially approved
q.why: ratified = 正式批准。

q.q: What does the writer mean by “children are not just people to be protected”?
opts: Children also have the right to be heard
Children do not really need any protection
Children should be the ones protecting adults
Children should be allowed to vote in elections
q.why: 第三段：They have the right to express their views。

q.q: Someone says: “Every country in the world has ratified the convention.” Based on the text, is this accurate?
opts: Yes — every country in the world has ratified it
Yes — and that includes Taiwan at the UN
No — every UN member except the US has ratified it
No — only eighteen countries have ratified it
q.why: 第四段：every UN member state except the United States。

tr.en: One of its most important ideas is that children are not just people to be protected.
tr.zh: 它最重要的觀念之一是：兒童不只是需要被保護的人。

tr.en: Taiwan, which is not a UN member, passed a law in 2014 to make the convention part of its own legal system.
tr.zh: 台灣雖然不是聯合國會員，仍在 2014 年通過法律，將這項公約納入自己的法律體系。

tr.en: Yet the gap between promise and reality remains wide.
tr.zh: 然而，承諾與現實之間的差距仍然很大。

tz: 1989 年 11 月 20 日，聯合國通過了《兒童權利公約》，這一天現在被定為世界兒童日來慶祝。
這項公約列出了每一位 18 歲以下的人，不論住在哪裡都應該享有的權利，包括受教育、獲得醫療照顧、免於暴力和剝削的保護，還有一條很有名的條文：休息和遊戲的權利。
它最重要的觀念之一是：孩子不只是需要被保護的人。他們有權利對影響自己的事情表達看法，而大人必須認真看待這些看法。
它已成為歷史上批准國家最多的人權條約：除了美國以外，每個聯合國會員國都已批准。不是聯合國會員的台灣，則在 2014 年通過一項法律，把這項公約納入自己的法律體系。
然而，承諾和現實之間的落差仍然很大。仍有數百萬名孩子沒有上學、從事危險的工作，或生活在戰爭之中。

ph.ex: The rules are set out on the first page.
ph.exzh: 規則列在第一頁。

ph.ex: Sunscreen gives you protection from the sun.
ph.exzh: 防曬乳能保護你不被曬傷。

ph.ex: Please take your homework seriously.
ph.exzh: 請認真看待你的作業。

ph.ex: She made reading part of her daily life.
ph.exzh: 她讓閱讀成為日常生活的一部分。

ph.ex: Millions of children are still out of school.
ph.exzh: 仍有數百萬名孩子失學。

c.title: Rights Before Adulthood
text: For most of history, children were regarded less as people than as possessions, or as adults in waiting. The Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted by the UN General Assembly on November 20, 1989, marked a decisive break with that view.

Its premise is that childhood carries rights of its own. Alongside protection from violence, exploitation and neglect, the convention guarantees education, health care and even rest and play, acknowledging that a good childhood is not merely survival.

Its most radical provision concerns participation: children have the right to express their views on matters affecting them, with due weight given according to their age and maturity. This reframes children from passive recipients of care into people whose opinions count.

The treaty has been ratified by every UN member except the United States, making it the most widely accepted human rights agreement ever. Taiwan, excluded from the UN, incorporated it into domestic law in 2014, an example of how norms can spread beyond formal membership.
Ratification, however, is not realisation. Child labour, conflict and unequal schooling persist, a reminder that rights written on paper become real only when adults choose to honour them.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Children are best understood as adults in waiting, not rights-holders.
The United States wrote the convention but chose not to ratify it.
Ratifying the treaty in 1989 largely solved the problem of child labour.
It treats children as rights-holders, but promises need adults to act.
q.why: 主旨：公約視兒童為權利主體並有發聲權，但承諾要靠行動實現。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “provision” means ___.
opts: food packed for a long journey
a part or rule of a legal agreement
a type of school for children
a promise made by children to their parents
q.why: provision = 條款。

q.q: Why does the writer call the participation right “radical”?
opts: It makes children people whose opinions count
It encourages children to use violence
Only adults are allowed to vote on it
It gives children the right to vote in national elections
q.why: 第三段：reframes children from passive recipients … into people whose opinions count。

q.q: What is the writer's attitude in the final paragraph?
opts: Satisfied that all of the work is now done
Angry at children for not using their rights
Realistic: signing is not making rights real
Uninterested in what happens next
q.why: Ratification, however, is not realisation——務實的提醒。

q.q: What does the example of Taiwan in paragraph 4 show?
opts: The UN directly controls Taiwan's laws
A norm can spread without UN membership
Taiwan rejected the treaty in 2014
The United States followed Taiwan's lead
q.why: 第四段：norms can spread beyond formal membership。

q.q: A city council plans to close a children's park without asking anyone. Based on the convention as described, what is the strongest objection?
opts: Parks cost the city a lot of money to keep open every year
Only adults really use the parks in most cities anyway
The council must first ask the United States for permission
Children have rights to play and to be heard on such decisions
q.why: 第二、三段：休息與遊戲的權利，以及對影響自己的事表達意見的權利。

tz: 在歷史上的大部分時間裡，孩子與其說是「人」，不如說被當成財產，或是「還沒長大的大人」。1989 年 11 月 20 日由聯合國大會通過的《兒童權利公約》，標誌著與這種看法的決定性決裂。
它的前提是：童年本身就帶有權利。除了免於暴力、剝削和疏忽的保護之外，公約也保障教育、醫療，甚至休息和遊戲——承認美好的童年不只是活下來而已。
它最具突破性的條款與「參與」有關：孩子有權利對影響他們的事情表達意見，並依照他們的年齡和成熟度給予應有的重視。這把孩子從被動接受照顧的人，重新定位為意見有分量的人。
除了美國以外，每個聯合國會員國都已批准這項條約，使它成為有史以來接受度最高的人權協定。被排除在聯合國之外的台灣，在 2014 年把它納入國內法——這個例子說明了規範可以擴散到正式會員資格之外。
然而，批准並不等於實現。童工、戰爭和不平等的教育依然存在，提醒我們：寫在紙上的權利，只有在大人選擇去尊重它們時，才會成真。

ph.ex: He is less a teacher than a friend to us.
ph.exzh: 對我們來說，他與其說是老師，不如說是朋友。

ph.ex: The new rule marked a break with the past.
ph.exzh: 這條新規定標誌著與過去的決裂。

ph.ex: Seats are given according to age.
ph.exzh: 座位依照年齡安排。

ph.ex: Her kindness makes her the most popular girl in class.
ph.exzh: 她的善良讓她成為班上最受歡迎的女生。
ph.m: making it the most widely accepted

ph.ex: The view was beautiful beyond words.
ph.exzh: 景色美得無法用言語形容。

ph.ex: You can choose to be kind every day.
ph.exzh: 你每天都可以選擇善良。

discuss: Which right in the convention do you think is the most important? Why?
Do adults at your school or home listen to children's opinions? Give an example.
What could students do to help children in other countries who cannot go to school?

topic: Fibonacci Day: The Numbers in Nature
zh: 費氏數列日：藏在大自然裡的數字
src: Science · National Geographic · The New York Times

text: November 23 is Fibonacci Day. The date 11/23 looks like the start of a famous number pattern: 1, 1, 2, 3.
In this pattern, you add the two numbers before to get the next one. So 1 + 1 = 2, 1 + 2 = 3, and 2 + 3 = 5.
The pattern is named after Fibonacci, an Italian man who wrote about it more than 800 years ago.
These numbers often appear in nature. Count the spirals on a sunflower or a pinecone, and you may find 8, 13, 21 or 34.
Fibonacci also helped people in Europe use the numbers we use today: 0 to 9.
Next time you see a flower, try counting. Maths might be hiding there!

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How to grow sunflowers
Fibonacci's life in Italy
A famous number pattern and where it appears
Why Fibonacci wrote about sunflowers in Italy
q.why: 全文介紹費氏數列與它在自然中的出現。

q.q: How do you get the next number in the pattern?
opts: Add the two numbers before it
Add 1 to the number before
Multiply the two numbers before it
Count the spirals on a flower
q.why: 第二段：you add the two numbers before to get the next one。

q.q: When did Fibonacci write about the pattern?
opts: On November 23
Last century
More than 2,000 years ago
More than 800 years ago
q.why: 第三段：more than 800 years ago。

q.q: In the text, a “pattern” is ___.
opts: a kind of flower
something that repeats in a regular way
a famous person
a number that is bigger than all the others
q.why: pattern = 規律、模式。

q.q: Why is November 23 Fibonacci Day?
opts: It is Fibonacci's birthday
11/23 looks like 1, 1, 2, 3
Sunflowers bloom that day
Fibonacci died that day
q.why: 第一段：11/23 looks like the start of … 1, 1, 2, 3。

q.q: The pattern goes 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… What is the next number?
q.why: 8 + 13 = 21（第二段的加法規則）。

gt.en: In this pattern, you add the two numbers before to get the next one.
gt.zh: 在這個規律裡，你把前面兩個數字相加，就得到下一個數字。

gt.en: These numbers often appear in nature.
gt.zh: 這些數字常常出現在大自然中。

gt.en: Next time you see a flower, try counting.
gt.zh: 下次你看到花的時候，試著數一數。

gt.en: Maths might be hiding there!
gt.zh: 數學可能就藏在那裡！

tz: 11 月 23 日是費波那契日。11/23 這個日期看起來像一串有名數列的開頭：1、1、2、3。
在這個數列裡，把前面兩個數字加起來，就得到下一個數字。所以 1 + 1 = 2，1 + 2 = 3，2 + 3 = 5。
這個數列以費波那契命名，他是一位義大利人，在八百多年前寫到了它。
這些數字常常出現在大自然裡。數一數向日葵或松果上的螺旋，你可能會數到 8、13、21 或 34。
費波那契也幫助歐洲人開始使用我們今天用的數字：0 到 9。
下次你看到一朵花，試著數一數。數學也許就藏在那裡！

ph.ex: Your handwriting looks like your mother's.
ph.exzh: 你的字跡看起來很像你媽媽的。

ph.ex: The street is named after a famous poet.
ph.exzh: 這條街以一位知名詩人命名。

ph.ex: Next time, bring an umbrella.
ph.exzh: 下次記得帶傘。

b.title: Rabbits, Sunflowers and a Famous Sequence
text: Every November 23, maths fans celebrate Fibonacci Day, because the date written as 11/23 matches the first four numbers of the Fibonacci sequence.

The sequence starts 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and each number is the sum of the two before it. It takes its name from Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, who described it in his book Liber Abaci in 1202 through a puzzle about breeding rabbits.

Fibonacci did not invent the sequence: Indian mathematicians had studied the same pattern centuries earlier. His bigger contribution was introducing the Hindu–Arabic numerals 0 to 9 to Europe, which made calculation far easier than Roman numerals.

The numbers appear surprisingly often in plants. Sunflower heads and pinecones usually have spirals that come in neighbouring Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55, an arrangement that packs seeds efficiently.

However, popular claims that the sequence is hidden in every famous building or 'perfect' face are usually exaggerated. Scientists warn that if you look hard enough, you can find patterns almost anywhere.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Indian mathematicians invented the numbers 0 to 9, and Fibonacci copied their sequence from a book in 1202.
Fibonacci invented the sequence through a rabbit puzzle, and it is hidden in every famous building and face over the following centuries.
The Fibonacci sequence, named after a medieval mathematician, really appears in plants, though some claims about it are exaggerated.
Roman numerals are easier than Hindu–Arabic numerals.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：數列的由來、在植物中的出現，以及被誇大的說法。

q.q: Which puzzle did Fibonacci use to describe the sequence?
opts: A puzzle about sunflower seeds
A puzzle about famous buildings
A puzzle about Roman numerals
A puzzle about breeding rabbits
q.why: 第二段：through a puzzle about breeding rabbits。

q.q: What was Fibonacci's bigger contribution, according to the text?
opts: Bringing the Hindu–Arabic numerals 0 to 9 to Europe
Inventing the sequence
Counting the spirals on sunflower heads and pinecones
Writing about Indian mathematicians
q.why: 第三段：His bigger contribution was introducing the Hindu–Arabic numerals。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “exaggerated” means ___.
opts: proved by scientists
made to seem bigger or more true than it really is
hidden in buildings
shown to be true by careful scientific measurement
q.why: exaggerated = 誇大的。

q.q: Why do sunflowers use spirals in Fibonacci numbers?
opts: Because Fibonacci planted them
Because rabbits eat them
Because the numbers look beautiful to the insects that visit
Because this arrangement packs seeds efficiently
q.why: 第四段：an arrangement that packs seeds efficiently。

q.q: A video says: “Every beautiful face follows the Fibonacci sequence exactly.” Based on the text, how should you judge this?
opts: Accept it, because the sequence is everywhere
Accept it, because Fibonacci studied faces
Be careful: the text says such claims are usually exaggerated
Reject it, because the sequence never appears anywhere in nature
q.why: 最後一段：popular claims … are usually exaggerated。

tr.en: Fibonacci did not invent the sequence: Indian mathematicians had studied the same pattern centuries earlier.
tr.zh: 費波那契並沒有發明這個數列：印度數學家早在幾百年前就研究過同樣的規律。

tr.en: The numbers appear surprisingly often in plants.
tr.zh: 這些數字出現在植物中的頻率令人驚訝。

tr.en: Scientists warn that if you look hard enough, you can find patterns almost anywhere.
tr.zh: 科學家提醒，只要你努力去找，幾乎在任何地方都能找到規律。

tz: 每年 11 月 23 日，數學迷都會慶祝費波那契日，因為寫成 11/23 的日期，正好對上費波那契數列的前四個數字。
這個數列從 1、1、2、3、5、8、13 開始，每個數字都是前兩個數字的和。它的名字來自比薩的李奧納多，也就是大家熟知的費波那契；他在 1202 年的著作《計算之書》裡，透過一道關於兔子繁殖的謎題描述了它。
費波那契並沒有發明這個數列：印度數學家在好幾個世紀前就研究過同樣的規律。他更大的貢獻，是把 0 到 9 的印度－阿拉伯數字引進歐洲，讓計算比使用羅馬數字容易得多。
這些數字出現在植物中的頻率高得驚人。向日葵的花盤和松果的螺旋數，通常是兩個相鄰的費波那契數，例如 34 和 55，這種排列能讓種子排得很緊密、有效率。
不過，那些宣稱這個數列藏在每一棟著名建築或「完美」臉孔裡的流行說法，通常都被誇大了。科學家提醒，只要找得夠用力，幾乎在任何地方都能找到規律。

ph.ex: The sum of 4 and 6 is 10.
ph.exzh: 4 加 6 的總和是 10。

ph.ex: The cake takes its name from the town where it was invented.
ph.exzh: 這種蛋糕的名字來自發明它的小鎮。

ph.ex: Riding a bike is far easier than I thought.
ph.exzh: 騎腳踏車比我想的容易得多。

ph.ex: I like fruits such as mangoes and grapes.
ph.exzh: 我喜歡芒果、葡萄之類的水果。

ph.ex: If you look hard enough, you can find good in everyone.
ph.exzh: 只要你夠用心找，每個人都有優點。

c.title: Patterns, Real and Imagined
text: Fibonacci Day, celebrated on November 23 because 11/23 echoes the opening of the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, honours one of mathematics' most beloved patterns, and offers a useful lesson in scepticism.

The rule is simple: each term is the sum of the two preceding ones. Leonardo of Pisa popularised it in Liber Abaci in 1202 through a whimsical problem about multiplying rabbits, though Indian scholars had described the same sequence far earlier. Ironically, his more consequential achievement was persuading European merchants to abandon cumbersome Roman numerals for the Hindu–Arabic system.

In botany the sequence earns its reputation. The spirals of sunflower heads and pinecones typically occur in adjacent Fibonacci numbers, because placing each new seed at a constant angle produces efficient packing; the mathematics emerges from growth rather than design.

Elsewhere, enthusiasm outruns evidence. Claims that the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa or ideal human faces encode the related golden ratio rarely survive careful measurement, and often depend on choosing convenient starting points.
The sequence therefore teaches two lessons at once: nature genuinely contains elegant regularities, and human minds are so eager for pattern that we readily invent ones that are not there.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: The sequence genuinely appears in plant growth, but many popular claims about it reflect our tendency to see patterns that aren't there.
Fibonacci's real achievement was the sequence itself, which Indian scholars had never described before 1202.
Fibonacci invented the sequence and the golden ratio.
The golden ratio is encoded in the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa and ideal faces, just as it is in sunflower spirals in exactly the same way everywhere.
q.why: 主旨：植物中確有規律，但許多說法反映人類愛找規律的傾向。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “cumbersome” means ___.
opts: ancient and beautiful
awkward and difficult to use
modern and fast
rare, valuable and difficult to find
q.why: cumbersome = 笨重麻煩的。

q.q: Why does the writer say the mathematics in sunflowers “emerges from growth rather than design”?
opts: Because a designer planned each flower
Because Fibonacci planted sunflowers
Because the pattern results naturally from seeds being placed at a constant angle as the plant grows
Because the pattern exists only in our minds, which are eager to find regular shapes everywhere in every case
q.why: 第三段：以固定角度生長自然產生，不是刻意設計。

q.q: How does the writer treat claims about the Parthenon and the Mona Lisa?
opts: As proven facts
As the strongest evidence that the sequence is found in everything
With no opinion
With scepticism, noting they rarely survive careful measurement
q.why: 第四段：rarely survive careful measurement。

q.q: How does the essay's structure support its final point?
opts: It lists only famous buildings
It contrasts a real example (plants) with doubtful ones (art) before concluding with two lessons
It tells Fibonacci's life story in order
It explains step by step how to calculate the golden ratio from the Fibonacci sequence in great detail
q.why: 先舉真實例子（植物），再舉可疑例子（藝術），最後得出兩個教訓。

q.q: A designer says her new logo is “scientifically perfect” because she found the golden ratio in it after trying many measurements. What is the best criticism?
opts: She may have chosen convenient starting points until she found the pattern she wanted
Logos cannot use maths
The golden ratio only appears in plants, so it can never be found in a designed logo
Fibonacci disliked logos
q.why: 第四段：often depend on choosing convenient starting points。

tz: 費波那契日在 11 月 23 日慶祝，因為 11/23 呼應了數列 1、1、2、3 的開頭；它紀念的是數學中最受喜愛的規律之一，也提供了一堂關於懷疑精神的實用課。
規則很簡單：每一項都是前兩項的和。比薩的李奧納多在 1202 年的《計算之書》中，透過一道關於兔子繁殖的奇想問題讓它廣為人知，不過印度學者更早就描述過同樣的數列。諷刺的是，他影響更深遠的成就，是說服歐洲商人放棄笨重的羅馬數字，改用印度－阿拉伯數字系統。
在植物學裡，這個數列的名聲是名副其實的。向日葵花盤和松果的螺旋，通常以相鄰的費波那契數出現，因為以固定角度擺放每一顆新種子，就能排列得最有效率；這種數學是從生長過程中產生的，而不是被設計出來的。
在其他地方，熱情就跑到證據前面去了。那些宣稱帕德嫩神殿、蒙娜麗莎或理想人臉裡藏著相關「黃金比例」的說法，很少經得起仔細測量，而且往往取決於挑選方便的起點。
因此，這個數列同時教了我們兩件事：大自然確實含有優雅的規律，而人類的大腦太渴望找到規律，以至於很容易就編造出根本不存在的規律。

ph.ex: The restaurant has earned its reputation for great noodles.
ph.exzh: 這家餐廳的好吃麵條名不虛傳。

ph.ex: He gave up soda for water.
ph.exzh: 他戒了汽水改喝水。

ph.ex: Few of his claims survive careful checking.
ph.exzh: 他的說法很少經得起仔細檢驗。

ph.ex: You can't do two things at once.
ph.exzh: 你不能同時做兩件事。

ph.ex: The children were eager for the holidays.
ph.exzh: 孩子們渴望放假。

Why do you think people love finding hidden patterns, even when they are not really there?

topic: Darwin's Big Book: On the Origin of Species
zh: 達爾文與《物種起源》
src: Natural History Museum · Nature · The Guardian

a.title: How Living Things Change
text: On November 24, 1859, a book called On the Origin of Species came out in England. It was written by Charles Darwin.
When he was young, Darwin sailed around the world on a ship called the Beagle. The trip took five years.
On the Galápagos Islands, he saw birds that looked a little different on each island. Their beaks were different shapes.
Darwin thought about this for many years. He believed living things change slowly over a very long time.
Animals and plants that fit their home better live longer and have more babies. He called this natural selection.
Many people were angry about his ideas at first. Today, his book is one of the most important science books ever.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A five-year trip on a ship
Birds on the Galápagos Islands
Why many people were angry about a five-year trip on a ship around the world
Darwin's famous book and his idea about how living things change
q.why: 全文介紹達爾文的書與他的演化觀念。

q.q: How long did Darwin's trip on the Beagle take?
opts: Five years
Five months
Twenty years
One year
q.why: 第二段：The trip took five years。

q.q: What did Darwin notice about the birds?
opts: They were all the same
They could not fly
Their beaks were different shapes on each island
They followed his ship from island to island every day
q.why: 第三段：Their beaks were different shapes。

q.q: In the text, “beaks” are ___.
opts: the wings of birds
the hard mouths of birds
the feathers of birds
ships
q.why: beaks = 鳥喙。

q.q: What does “natural selection” mean in the text?
opts: People choose the best animals
Darwin chose the strongest birds on each island to have more babies
Darwin chose which birds to study
Living things that fit their home better survive and have more babies
q.why: 第五段的說明。

q.q: On a snowy island, white rabbits are harder for foxes to see than brown rabbits. Based on Darwin's idea, what will probably happen over many years?
opts: Brown rabbits will become more common
White rabbits will become more common
All rabbits will disappear
Foxes will turn white
q.why: 第五段：更適應環境的白兔較能存活、繁殖。

gt.en: The trip took five years.
gt.zh: 這趟旅程花了五年。

gt.en: Their beaks were different shapes.
gt.zh: 牠們的鳥喙形狀不一樣。

gt.en: He believed living things change slowly over a very long time.
gt.zh: 他相信生物在非常長的時間裡慢慢改變。

gt.en: Many people were angry about his ideas at first.
gt.zh: 一開始很多人對他的想法很生氣。

tz: 1859 年 11 月 24 日，一本叫做《物種起源》的書在英國出版。作者是查爾斯・達爾文。
達爾文年輕時，搭著一艘叫做小獵犬號的船環遊世界。這趟旅程花了五年。
在加拉巴哥群島上，他看到每座島上的鳥看起來都有點不一樣。牠們的鳥喙形狀不同。
達爾文思考這件事思考了很多年。他相信生物會在非常漫長的時間裡慢慢改變。
比較適應自己生活環境的動物和植物，活得比較久，也生下比較多的後代。他把這叫做「天擇」。
一開始，許多人對他的想法很生氣。今天，他的書是有史以來最重要的科學書籍之一。

ph.ex: Her new book comes out next month.
ph.exzh: 她的新書下個月出版。

ph.ex: One day I want to sail around the world.
ph.exzh: 有一天我想航行環遊世界。

ph.ex: Think about it before you answer.
ph.exzh: 回答之前先想一想。

ph.ex: These shoes fit me better.
ph.exzh: 這雙鞋比較合我的腳。

b.title: The Book That Changed Biology
text: On November 24, 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species. The first printing sold out almost immediately, and the book went on to transform how people understand life on Earth.

Darwin's ideas had been forming for more than twenty years. As a young naturalist on the survey ship HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836, he collected fossils and observed animals in South America and on the Galápagos Islands, where species differed slightly from island to island.

His central idea was natural selection. Individuals vary, and those with traits that suit their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so over many generations species gradually change.

Darwin delayed publishing, partly because he knew his ideas would be controversial. He finally acted in 1858 when another naturalist, Alfred Russel Wallace, sent him a paper describing almost the same theory. Their work was presented together in London that year.
Today evolution is the foundation of modern biology, supported by evidence from fossils and DNA.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836.
Darwin's 1859 book explained natural selection, a theory that became the foundation of modern biology.
Wallace wrote On the Origin of Species.
Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle proved that species never change, which became the basis of modern biology.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：1859 年的書提出天擇，成為現代生物學基礎。

q.q: What did Darwin notice on the Galápagos Islands?
opts: There were no animals
The animals were exactly the same on every island
The islands had no plants
Species differed slightly from island to island
q.why: 第二段：species differed slightly from island to island。

q.q: What made Darwin finally publish his ideas?
opts: Wallace sent him a paper with almost the same theory
His ship returned in 1836
The book sold out
DNA evidence finally proved his ideas were correct
q.why: 第四段：Wallace sent him a paper describing almost the same theory。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “traits” are ___.
opts: the islands and seas where a species lives
old books
features or qualities of a living thing
islands
q.why: traits = 特徵。

q.q: Why might Darwin have delayed publishing for so long?
opts: He was too busy sailing
He had collected no fossils or evidence
Wallace asked him to wait
He knew his ideas would be controversial
q.why: 第四段：he knew his ideas would be controversial。

q.q: A quiz says: “Darwin alone came up with the theory of natural selection.” Based on the text, what is the best correction?
opts: Not quite: Wallace developed almost the same theory, and their work was presented together
Correct, Wallace only copied him
Correct: Wallace only read Darwin's book and then copied the theory in 1859 a few years later
Wrong, because Darwin never studied animals
q.why: 第四段：華萊士提出幾乎相同的理論，兩人的研究同年一起發表。

tr.en: His central idea was natural selection.
tr.zh: 他的核心觀念是天擇。

tr.en: Darwin delayed publishing, partly because he knew his ideas would be controversial.
tr.zh: 達爾文延後出版，部分原因是他知道自己的想法會引起爭議。

tr.en: Today evolution is the foundation of modern biology, supported by evidence from fossils and DNA.
tr.zh: 如今，演化是現代生物學的基礎，並有化石和 DNA 的證據支持。

tz: 1859 年 11 月 24 日，查爾斯・達爾文出版了《物種起源》。第一刷幾乎立刻就賣光了，這本書後來徹底改變了人們對地球生命的理解。
達爾文的想法已經醞釀了二十多年。1831 到 1836 年間，年輕的博物學家達爾文搭乘測量船小獵犬號，在南美洲和加拉巴哥群島收集化石、觀察動物；在那些島上，物種在不同的島之間略有差異。
他的核心想法是「天擇」。個體之間有差異，而擁有適合環境特徵的個體，比較可能存活並繁殖，所以經過許多世代，物種就會逐漸改變。
達爾文延後了出版，一部分原因是他知道自己的想法會引起爭議。1858 年，另一位博物學家阿爾弗雷德・羅素・華萊士寄給他一篇論文，描述幾乎相同的理論，他才終於採取行動。那一年，兩人的研究在倫敦一起發表。
今天，演化是現代生物學的基礎，並得到化石和 DNA 證據的支持。

ph.ex: The concert tickets sold out in minutes.
ph.exzh: 演唱會門票幾分鐘就賣光了。

ph.ex: Ferries travel from island to island.
ph.exzh: 渡輪在一座座島之間往來。

ph.ex: Over many generations, the language changed.
ph.exzh: 經過許多世代，這種語言改變了。

ph.ex: I was late, partly because of the rain.
ph.exzh: 我遲到了，部分是因為下雨。

ph.ex: The plan is supported by most parents.
ph.exzh: 這個計畫受到大部分家長支持。

c.title: The Long Patience of a Revolutionary
text: On November 24, 1859, a cautious naturalist published one of the most consequential books ever written. On the Origin of Species argued that the diversity of life arose not through separate acts of creation but through descent with modification, driven by natural selection.

The argument had been decades in the making. Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle in the 1830s furnished him with puzzles, notably the subtly different finches and tortoises of the Galápagos Islands, but he spent the next twenty years accumulating evidence, breeding pigeons and corresponding with experts before daring to publish.

That reluctance was strategic as well as temperamental. He anticipated fierce religious and scientific opposition, and he wanted his case to be overwhelming. Only a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace in 1858, outlining the same mechanism, forced his hand.

The book's power lay in its accumulation of ordinary observations into an extraordinary conclusion. Variation exists; more offspring are born than can survive; those best suited to their surroundings leave more descendants. Given immense time, small differences add up to new species.
Later discoveries in genetics, unknown to Darwin, supplied the mechanism of inheritance he lacked and confirmed the theory's core with striking precision.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Darwin published quickly after his voyage.
Darwin rushed his book into print after his voyage, and genetics later showed that most of his theory was wrong in the end.
Darwin's carefully delayed book built ordinary observations into a revolutionary theory later confirmed by genetics.
Darwin understood genetics fully.
q.why: 主旨：謹慎延後出版、由平凡觀察推出革命性結論，後被遺傳學證實。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “reluctance” means ___.
opts: unwillingness or hesitation
great excitement and hurry
religious belief
a scientific tool
q.why: reluctance = 遲疑、不情願。

q.q: Why did Darwin want his case to be “overwhelming”?
opts: Because Wallace asked him to
Because he wanted to sell more books
Because he had little evidence
Because he expected strong opposition
q.why: 第三段：He anticipated fierce religious and scientific opposition。

q.q: How does the writer view Darwin's long delay?
opts: As laziness
As cautious and strategic
As a mistake that cost him the theory
As fear of travel
q.why: 第三段：strategic as well as temperamental。

q.q: What is the role of paragraph 4?
opts: To summarise the simple steps of the argument that lead to a powerful conclusion
To list the book's sales figures
To describe the finches and tortoises that Darwin saw on the Galápagos Islands
To introduce genetics
q.why: 第四段濃縮天擇論證的步驟。

q.q: Someone argues: “Darwin didn't know about genes, so his theory must be wrong.” Based on the essay, what is the best response?
opts: Agree, because genes are essential
Agree: without knowing about genes, Darwin could not explain how species change at all
Disagree: later genetics supplied the missing mechanism and confirmed the theory's core
Disagree, because genes don't exist
q.why: 最後一段：遺傳學補上機制並證實理論核心。

tz: 1859 年 11 月 24 日，一位行事謹慎的博物學家出版了一本史上影響最深遠的書之一。《物種起源》主張，生命的多樣性並不是來自一次次各別的創造，而是透過「伴隨修改的傳承」，由天擇所推動。
這個論證醞釀了好幾十年。1830 年代搭乘小獵犬號的航行，給了達爾文許多謎題，特別是加拉巴哥群島上那些有細微差異的雀鳥和陸龜；但他接下來花了二十年累積證據、養鴿子、和專家通信，才敢出版。
這份遲疑既出於個性，也是一種策略。他預料到會有來自宗教和科學界的激烈反對，所以希望自己的論證壓倒性地充分。直到 1858 年阿爾弗雷德・羅素・華萊士寄來一封信，概述了同樣的機制，才逼得他不得不出手。
這本書的力量，在於把許多平凡的觀察累積成一個非凡的結論：個體之間存在差異；出生的後代比能活下來的多；最適應環境的個體會留下更多後代。只要有極長的時間，小小的差異就會累積成新的物種。
後來達爾文所不知道的遺傳學發現，補上了他所欠缺的遺傳機制，也以驚人的精確度證實了這個理論的核心。

Why do you think new scientific ideas sometimes make people angry?

topic: Andrew Carnegie: From Poor Boy to Library Builder
zh: 卡內基：從窮小子到圖書館之父
src: Carnegie Corporation · The Economist · The Washington Post

a.title: The Rich Man Who Gave Libraries
text: Andrew Carnegie was born on November 25, 1835, in Scotland. His family was very poor.
When he was 12, his family moved to America. Andrew started working in a factory and earned very little money.
He worked hard and learned quickly. Later, he started a steel company and became one of the richest people in the world.
But Carnegie believed rich people should give their money to help others.
He gave money to build more than 2,500 public libraries. Many poor children, like he was, could now read books for free.
Some workers in his factories, however, were paid little and worked in dangerous places. People still discuss both sides of his story.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A poor boy who became rich and gave money for libraries
How steel is made
Why factories are dangerous
A poor family who stayed in Scotland and built steel
q.why: 全文介紹卡內基從貧窮到富有、捐建圖書館。

q.q: How old was Andrew when his family moved to America?
q.why: 第二段：When he was 12。

q.q: How many public libraries did he help build?
opts: About 25
More than 2,500
More than 250
Exactly 1,835
q.why: 第五段：more than 2,500 public libraries。

q.q: In the text, “public” libraries are libraries that ___.
opts: only rich people can use
sell books
everyone can use
are in factories
q.why: public = 公共的，人人可用。

q.q: Why did libraries matter so much to Carnegie?
opts: He remembered being a poor child who needed free books
He wanted to sell books
He wanted to sell books to the children of his workers
Libraries made steel
q.why: 第五段：Many poor children, like he was, could now read books for free。

q.q: Your friend says, “Carnegie was a perfect hero.” Based on the text, what is a fair reply?
opts: Yes, everyone agrees
No, he never gave any money
Yes, because he gave money to build more than 2,500 libraries around the world
He did a lot of good, but some workers were paid little and worked in danger
q.why: 最後一段：People still discuss both sides of his story。

gt.en: His family was very poor.
gt.zh: 他的家庭非常貧窮。

gt.en: He worked hard and learned quickly.

tz: 安德魯・卡內基 1835 年 11 月 25 日出生於蘇格蘭。他的家庭非常貧窮。
他 12 歲時，全家搬到美國。安德魯開始在工廠工作，賺的錢非常少。
他工作努力、學得很快。後來他創立了一家鋼鐵公司，成為世界上最富有的人之一。
但是卡內基相信，有錢人應該把錢拿出來幫助別人。
他捐錢蓋了超過 2,500 座公共圖書館。許多像他小時候一樣貧窮的孩子，現在可以免費讀書了。
不過，他工廠裡有些工人薪水很低，而且在危險的地方工作。人們至今仍在討論他故事的兩面。

ph.exzh: 我們去年搬到台中。

ph.ex: Children learn quickly when they play.
ph.exzh: 孩子們在玩的時候學得很快。

ph.ex: She gives her time to help old people.

b.title: Making a Fortune, Giving It Away
text: Andrew Carnegie, born on November 25, 1835, in Dunfermline, Scotland, is one of history's most famous examples of rags to riches.

His family emigrated to Pittsburgh in 1848, where twelve-year-old Andrew worked in a cotton mill for little more than a dollar a week. He moved on to a job as a telegraph messenger, impressed his bosses, and invested his savings wisely.
By the 1870s he had built a steel empire. In 1901 he sold Carnegie Steel for about 480 million dollars, making him one of the richest men alive.

Carnegie then devoted himself to giving his fortune away. In his essay The Gospel of Wealth, he argued that the rich have a duty to use their money for the public good during their lifetimes. He funded more than 2,500 public libraries around the world, as well as universities and concert halls.
His record is mixed, however. In 1892 a bitter strike at his Homestead steelworks ended in deadly violence, and critics argue that his generosity was paid for by workers' low wages and long hours.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Carnegie rose from poverty to great wealth and gave much of it away, though his record is mixed.
Carnegie sold his company for 480 million dollars.
Carnegie wrote only about libraries.
Carnegie became rich by building public libraries, and his workers were always paid high wages.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：白手起家、大量捐獻，但評價兩極。

q.q: What was Carnegie's first job in Pittsburgh?
opts: Telegraph messenger
Working in a cotton mill
Running a steel company
Building libraries
q.why: 第二段：worked in a cotton mill for little more than a dollar a week。

q.q: What did The Gospel of Wealth argue?
opts: The rich should save all their money
Workers should be paid more
The rich have a duty to use their money for the public good while alive
Workers should share the company's money while the rich are still alive
q.why: 第四段的說明。

q.q: In paragraph 5, a “strike” is ___.
opts: a type of steel
a gift of money
a hit with a hammer in a steel factory in Pittsburgh
a time when workers stop working to protest
q.why: strike = 罷工。

q.q: Why do critics say his generosity was “paid for” by workers?
opts: Workers donated the libraries
His fortune came partly from workers' low wages and long hours
Workers built the libraries for free
Workers gave part of their wages to help build the libraries
q.why: 最後一段：paid for by workers' low wages and long hours。

q.q: A school poster says: “Carnegie: The Workers' Best Friend.” Based on the text, is this accurate?
opts: Yes, he paid the highest wages
Yes, because he worked in a cotton mill himself and understood workers
No, because he never owned factories
No, the Homestead strike and low wages suggest a more complicated record
q.why: 最後一段：His record is mixed。

tr.en: By the 1870s he had built a steel empire.
tr.zh: 到了 1870 年代，他已經建立起一個鋼鐵帝國。

tr.en: Carnegie then devoted himself to giving his fortune away.
tr.zh: 之後卡內基致力於把自己的財富捐出去。

tr.zh: 然而，他的評價好壞參半。

tz: 安德魯・卡內基 1835 年 11 月 25 日生於蘇格蘭的丹弗姆林，是歷史上最有名的「白手起家」例子之一。
他的家人在 1848 年移民到匹茲堡，十二歲的安德魯在一家棉紡廠工作，一週只賺一美元多一點。後來他換到電報送信員的工作，讓上司印象深刻，並把積蓄做了聰明的投資。
到了 1870 年代，他已經建立起一個鋼鐵帝國。1901 年，他以大約 4.8 億美元賣掉卡內基鋼鐵公司，成為當時世上最富有的人之一。
之後卡內基致力於把財富捐出去。他在文章《財富的福音》中主張，富人有責任在有生之年把錢用在公共利益上。他資助了全世界超過 2,500 座公共圖書館，還有大學和音樂廳。
不過，他的紀錄有好有壞。1892 年，他旗下霍姆斯特德鋼鐵廠的一場激烈罷工以致命的暴力收場；批評者認為，他的慷慨是用工人的低薪和長工時換來的。

ph.zh: 白手起家、從貧窮到富有
ph.ex: His life is a true rags-to-riches story.
ph.exzh: 他的一生是一個真正的白手起家故事。

ph.ex: After the test, we moved on to the next chapter.
ph.exzh: 考完試後，我們接著上下一章。

ph.ex: She devoted herself to helping animals.
ph.exzh: 她致力於幫助動物。

ph.ex: We have a duty to protect our planet.
ph.exzh: 我們有責任保護地球。

ph.ex: The trip was paid for by the school.
ph.exzh: 這趟旅行由學校出錢。

c.title: The Contradictions of a Philanthropist
text: Andrew Carnegie, born in Scotland on November 25, 1835, embodied the American myth of the self-made man with almost theatrical neatness: a penniless immigrant boy who became the richest industrialist of his age.

His ascent combined diligence, shrewd investment and fortunate timing. From a cotton mill and a telegraph office he rose into railways and then steel, ruthlessly cutting costs until Carnegie Steel dominated the industry. Its sale in 1901 for roughly 480 million dollars made him almost unimaginably wealthy.

What followed was equally remarkable. In The Gospel of Wealth he contended that dying rich was a disgrace and that fortunes should be distributed for the public good. He funded more than 2,500 libraries, believing that access to knowledge, not charity handouts, allowed people to improve themselves.

Yet the same cost-cutting that built the fortune also produced the Homestead strike of 1892, in which a clash between strikers and armed guards left several people dead. Critics then and since have asked whether generosity can redeem wealth extracted from exhausted workers.
Carnegie's legacy thus resists a simple verdict, and it raises a question that remains urgent: should society rely on the goodwill of the very rich, or on fairer wages in the first place?

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Carnegie's life combined remarkable philanthropy with harsh labour practices, raising the question of whether charity can replace fair wages.
Carnegie was simply a generous hero.
Carnegie's libraries caused the Homestead strike.
Carnegie's libraries made up for the Homestead strike, proving that generous gifts can fully replace fair wages for workers in his company.
q.why: 主旨：慈善與嚴苛勞動並存，引出「靠富人善意還是公平薪資」的問題。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “shrewd” means ___.
opts: lazy
clever in practical matters
generous
dishonest and cruel to others
q.why: shrewd = 精明的。

q.q: Why did Carnegie prefer funding libraries to giving charity handouts?
opts: Libraries were cheaper to build than paying higher wages for his companies
Handouts were illegal
Workers asked for libraries
He believed access to knowledge helped people improve themselves
q.why: 第三段：access to knowledge, not charity handouts, allowed people to improve themselves。

q.q: How does the writer judge Carnegie's legacy?
opts: As purely good, because he gave money away
As purely bad
As complex, resisting a simple verdict
As unimportant
q.why: 最後一段：resists a simple verdict。

q.q: What is the function of “Yet” at the start of paragraph 4?
opts: To add more praise for the libraries he built around the world in Pittsburgh
To turn from his generosity to the darker side of how the fortune was made
To introduce a new person
To summarise his libraries
q.why: Yet 轉向財富來源的陰暗面。

q.q: A billionaire today pays workers very little but donates millions to schools. Which question does the essay suggest we should ask?
opts: Would it be fairer to pay workers better in the first place, instead of relying on donations?
Which schools got the most money?
Is the billionaire Scottish?
How many libraries could the billionaire build with the same money as Carnegie? in each city
q.why: 最後一段：should society rely on the goodwill of the very rich, or on fairer wages？

tz: 1835 年 11 月 25 日生於蘇格蘭的安德魯・卡內基，幾乎像演戲一樣完美地體現了美國「白手起家」的神話：一個身無分文的移民男孩，成為他那個時代最富有的實業家。
他的崛起結合了勤奮、精明的投資和好時機。他從棉紡廠和電報局起步，進入鐵路業，再進入鋼鐵業，毫不留情地壓低成本，直到卡內基鋼鐵公司稱霸整個產業。1901 年以約 4.8 億美元出售公司，讓他富有到幾乎難以想像。
接下來發生的事同樣驚人。他在《財富的福音》中主張，富有地死去是一種恥辱，財富應該為了公共利益而分配出去。他資助了超過 2,500 座圖書館，相信讓人們取得知識，而不是發放救濟，才能讓人改善自己的生活。
然而，打造這筆財富的同一套成本壓縮手段，也造成了 1892 年的霍姆斯特德罷工：罷工工人和武裝警衛之間的衝突造成數人死亡。當時和後來的批評者都在問：慷慨捐贈，能否彌補從精疲力竭的工人身上榨取來的財富？
因此，卡內基的歷史定位無法簡單下結論，而它也提出一個至今仍然迫切的問題：社會應該依靠超級富豪的善意，還是從一開始就給予更公平的工資？

ph.zh: 晉升到、進入（更高的領域）

ph.exzh: 她晉升到公司的高層職位。

ph.exzh: 接下來是一整週的大雨。

ph.exzh: 浪費這麼多食物是一種恥辱。

ph.exzh: 這場暴風雨造成三人死亡。

topic: Charles Schulz and the World of Peanuts
zh: 舒茲與《花生漫畫》：史努比的爸爸
src: Charles M. Schulz Museum · The New York Times · NBC

a.title: The Man Who Drew Snoopy
text: Charles Schulz was born on November 26, 1922, in the United States. He loved drawing from a young age.
In 1950, he started a comic strip called Peanuts. It showed a shy boy named Charlie Brown and his dog, Snoopy.
Charlie Brown often failed. He could never kick the football, and his kite always got stuck in a tree. But he never gave up.
Snoopy was very different. He had a big imagination and pretended to be a pilot, a writer and much more.
Schulz drew Peanuts by himself for almost 50 years, nearly 18,000 comic strips!
Today, people all over the world still love Snoopy and his friends.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How to fly a kite
A dog named Snoopy who was a real pilot in the sky
Charles Schulz and his famous comic, Peanuts
Why Charlie Brown is shy
q.why: 全文介紹舒茲與《花生漫畫》。

q.q: When did Peanuts start?
opts: In 1922 on November 26
Almost 50 years ago
q.why: 第二段：In 1950, he started a comic strip called Peanuts。

q.q: What did Snoopy pretend to be?
opts: A pilot and a writer
A football player
A teacher
Charlie Brown
q.why: 第四段：pretended to be a pilot, a writer and much more。

q.q: In the text, “imagination” means ___.
opts: a kind of comic
the ability to kick a football very far in a big game
being shy
the ability to make pictures and ideas in your mind
q.why: imagination = 想像力。

q.q: What can we learn from Charlie Brown?
opts: Never try new things
Dogs are better than people
Kites are dangerous
Keep trying even when you fail
q.why: 第三段：he often failed … But he never gave up。

q.q: Your little brother keeps failing to ride a bike and wants to quit. How could you use Charlie Brown's story?
opts: Tell him to give up like Charlie Brown
Tell him to get a dog instead
Tell him Charlie Brown failed many times but never gave up
Tell him Charlie Brown finally learned to ride a bike in the end
q.why: 第三段：查理布朗屢敗卻不放棄。

gt.en: He loved drawing from a young age.

gt.en: But he never gave up.

gt.en: Today, people all over the world still love Snoopy and his friends.

tz: 查爾斯・舒茲在 1922 年 11 月 26 日出生於美國。他從小就很喜歡畫畫。
1950 年，他開始畫一部叫做《花生》的漫畫。漫畫裡有一個害羞的男孩叫查理・布朗，還有他的狗史努比。
查理・布朗常常失敗。他永遠踢不到那顆足球，他的風箏也總是卡在樹上。但他從不放棄。
史努比非常不一樣。牠的想像力很豐富，會假裝自己是飛行員、作家，還有很多其他角色。
舒茲一個人畫了《花生》將近 50 年，一共差不多 18,000 則漫畫！
今天，全世界的人仍然很喜歡史努比和牠的朋友們。

b.title: Good Grief: The Genius of Peanuts
text: Charles M. Schulz, born in Minneapolis on November 26, 1922, created one of the most popular comic strips in history. Peanuts first appeared in newspapers on October 2, 1950, and ran for almost fifty years.
Unusually, Schulz wrote, drew and lettered every one of the nearly 18,000 strips himself, without assistants.

His characters were children, but their worries were very adult. Charlie Brown is lonely and unlucky; Lucy is bossy; Linus carries a security blanket while thinking deep thoughts. Readers recognised their own fears and disappointments in these small figures.
Snoopy, Charlie Brown's beagle, provided the fantasy. Lying on top of his doghouse, he imagines himself as a fighter pilot or a famous novelist.
The strip grew into books, toys and television specials such as A Charlie Brown Christmas in 1965.
Schulz died in February 2000, just hours before his final Sunday strip was published. Today, his gentle mix of sadness and humour continues to influence cartoonists around the world.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Schulz's Peanuts became hugely popular by showing children with very human worries, mixed with gentle humour and fantasy.
Peanuts first appeared on October 2, 1950.
Peanuts was popular because Snoopy was a real fighter pilot and famous novelist who always won in every single strip he appeared in.
Schulz used many assistants.
q.why: 涵蓋全文：兒童角色、成人般的煩惱、幽默與幻想。

q.q: What was unusual about how Schulz made the strip?
opts: He used dozens of assistants
He did all the writing and drawing himself
He only drew the Sunday strips himself for newspapers
He wrote it for television first
q.why: 第二段：drew and lettered every one … himself, without assistants。

q.q: Which character carries a security blanket?
opts: Lucy
Charlie Brown
Snoopy
Linus
q.why: 第三段：Linus carries a security blanket。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “bossy” describes someone who ___.
opts: is very shy
is always lucky
likes telling others what to do
always loses at baseball in every game
q.why: bossy = 愛指揮人的。

q.q: Why did readers connect with the children in Peanuts?
opts: Because the children were famous
Because the strips were very long
Because the children always won their baseball games every week
Because they saw their own fears and disappointments in them
q.why: 第三段：Readers recognised their own fears and disappointments。

q.q: A headline says: “Schulz Retired Years Before His Death.” Based on the text, is this accurate?
opts: Yes, he stopped drawing after A Charlie Brown Christmas in 1965
Yes, assistants drew the last strips
No, his final strip was published just hours after he died in 2000
No, he never stopped drawing until 2010
q.why: 最後一段：died … just hours before his final Sunday strip was published。

tr.en: His characters were children, but their worries were very adult.
tr.zh: 他筆下的角色是孩子，但他們的煩惱很成人。

tr.en: Snoopy, Charlie Brown's beagle, provided the fantasy.
